title: The Shogun's System of Alternate Attendance
text:
After the Tokugawa won control of Japan in the early 1600s, the shoguns faced a basic problem: around two hundred and fifty regional lords, the daimyo, still had their own lands, revenues and samurai. Several had fought against the Tokugawa only a generation before.

In 1635 the third shogun, Tokugawa Iemitsu, revised the Laws for the Military Houses and made a practice that had grown up informally into a formal obligation, known as sankin kotai, alternate attendance. Most daimyo had to spend every other year in the shogun's capital of Edo and the alternate year in their home domains. Their wives and heirs had to live in Edo permanently.

The system worked in several ways at once. The families in Edo were in effect hostages. The lords had to maintain grand residences in the capital, and travel to and from it in large processions that matched their rank, sometimes with thousands of retainers. These costs consumed a large share of each domain's income, leaving less money for armies or plots. And lords who spent half their lives at the shogun's court were drawn into its culture and rivalries rather than building power at home.

The system lasted more than two centuries, a period with no major civil war. It also had side effects nobody planned: roads, inns and trade along the highways flourished, and Edo grew into one of the largest cities in the world.
lesson: You can tame rivals not only with force but by shaping their obligations, so that their resources and attention are absorbed by the system itself.
source: Buke Shohatto (Laws for the Military Houses), revision of 1635; Constantine Vaporis, Tour of Duty (2008)
